## Learning Objectives

After this chapter, you will be able to:

::: {.incremental}
- Explain **belief updating** in plain language -- "updating your best guess when you learn something new"
- Compute **marginal probabilities** by averaging across possibilities you have not yet observed
- Trace how **evidence flows** through chains, forks, and colliders -- and know when the flow stops
- Apply the **explaining away** phenomenon -- the crown jewel of causal inference -- to real health-system puzzles
- Use a Bayesian network to **diagnose** why an Ethiopian region has high neonatal mortality
:::

::: {.callout-box}
**The big idea:** In Chapter 4 we built the model *forward* -- starting from causes and predicting outcomes. Now we run it **backwards**. We see the outcome and ask: *What caused this?* This is how managers, doctors, and detectives actually think.
:::


# The Detective's Question {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">You see the outcome. Now work backwards to figure out what caused it.</span>


## The Wet Sidewalk

You walk outside and the sidewalk is wet. What happened?

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box}
**Possibility 1: It rained.**

Rain would explain the wet sidewalk. But you were asleep, so you did not see it.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Possibility 2: The sprinklers went off.**

The neighbor's sprinkler system runs at 5 AM. That could also explain it.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**This is the detective's question.** You see the result (wet sidewalk). You did not see the cause. You have to reason *backwards* -- from effect to cause -- using what you know about how the world works.
:::


## The Same Logic, Applied to Health

Here is the detective question for a health program manager:

. . .

::: {.example-block}
[The Manager's Puzzle]{.example-label}

An Ethiopian region reports a neonatal mortality rate of 35 per 1,000 live births -- well above the national average of about 28 per 1,000. The program director asks:

**"What is most likely going wrong? Is it staffing? Equipment? The referral system? All three?"**

You cannot visit every facility. But you have a model. You can run it backwards.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
This chapter teaches you the mechanics of running the model backwards. There are exactly three skills: averaging across possibilities, updating your best guess, and understanding how evidence flows through different structures.
:::


## From Forward to Backward

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box}
**Chapter 4 (Forward)**

Given causes, predict effects:

"*If* staffing is low and equipment is unavailable, *what is the probability* of high mortality?"

Direction: Cause --> Effect
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Chapter 5 (Backward)**

Given effects, infer causes:

"We *observe* high mortality in a region. *What does this tell us* about staffing and equipment?"

Direction: Effect --> Cause
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
Both directions use the same model. The math is the same. The difference is what you know and what you want to find out.
:::


# Averaging Across Possibilities {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">If you do not know the cause, average across the possibilities</span>


## When You Do Not Know

Suppose you want to predict mortality in a region, but you have no idea whether staffing is adequate or low.

. . .

::: {.example-block}
[A Simple Two-Option Example]{.example-label}

You know two things from your model:

- If staffing is **adequate**, probability of high mortality = 20%
- If staffing is **low**, probability of high mortality = 55%

And you know from national data that about 40% of Ethiopian health facilities have adequate staffing.
:::

. . .

So what is your overall best guess for mortality?

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**You average across the two possibilities, weighted by how likely each one is:**

Overall P(High Mortality) = 0.40 x 0.20 + 0.60 x 0.55 = 0.08 + 0.33 = **0.41**

Your best guess is a 41% chance of high mortality -- a weighted average of the two scenarios.
:::


## The Weighted Average in Pictures

Think of it like mixing two buckets of paint:

. . .

| Scenario | How Likely? | P(High Mortality) | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Staffing = Adequate | 40% | 20% | 0.40 x 0.20 = 0.08 |
| Staffing = Low | 60% | 55% | 0.60 x 0.55 = 0.33 |
| **Overall** | **100%** | | **0.41** |

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**The fancy name for this is "marginal probability."** It means the overall probability of something when you do not know -- and therefore average across -- one or more other variables. But "weighted average across possibilities" is all it really is.
:::


## Averaging with Two Unknown Parents

Now suppose you also do not know whether equipment is available. You average across *all four* combinations:

. . .

| Staffing | Equipment | Weight | P(High Mortality) | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adequate | Available | 0.40 x 0.35 = 0.14 | 0.15 | 0.021 |
| Adequate | Unavailable | 0.40 x 0.65 = 0.26 | 0.30 | 0.078 |
| Low | Available | 0.60 x 0.35 = 0.21 | 0.40 | 0.084 |
| Low | Unavailable | 0.60 x 0.65 = 0.39 | 0.60 | 0.234 |
| | | **1.00** | | **0.417** |

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**P(High Mortality) = 41.7% before we learn anything about this region.**

This is our starting point -- our "before" number. Everything that follows is about how this number changes when evidence comes in.
:::


# Updating Your Best Guess {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">New evidence shifts your beliefs</span>


## Before and After

Here is the core idea of this chapter, in one sentence:

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**When you learn something new, your estimates change.**

Your "before" beliefs are called the **prior**. Your "after" beliefs -- after incorporating evidence -- are called the **posterior**. The shift from prior to posterior is **belief updating**.
:::

. . .

::: {.example-block}
[Wet Sidewalk, Revisited]{.example-label}

- **Before** looking outside: 50% chance it rained last night (your prior)
- You look outside and see the sidewalk is wet
- **After** seeing the wet sidewalk: 75% chance it rained (your posterior)

The wet sidewalk shifted your belief by 25 percentage points.
:::


## Updating in the MNH Model

Let us apply this to a real problem.

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box}
**BEFORE (Prior)**

We know nothing about this specific Ethiopian region.

- P(Staffing = Low) = **60%**
- P(Equipment = Unavailable) = **65%**

These are national averages from Ethiopia's HMIS data.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**AFTER (Posterior)**

We learn the region has **high neonatal mortality**.

- P(Staffing = Low | High NMR) = **73%**
- P(Equipment = Unavailable | High NMR) = **74%**

Both bad explanations became more likely.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**What just happened?** High mortality is *more consistent* with low staffing than with adequate staffing. So observing high mortality shifts our belief toward the "low staffing" explanation. The same logic applies to equipment.
:::


## How Much Does Evidence Shift Your Beliefs?

The size of the shift depends on how *diagnostic* the evidence is:

. . .

| Variable | Prior | Posterior (given NMR=High) | Shift |
|---|---|---|---|
| P(Staffing = Low) | 0.60 | 0.73 | **+13 points** |
| P(Equipment = Unavailable) | 0.65 | 0.74 | **+9 points** |
| P(Referral = Weak) | 0.50 | 0.58 | **+8 points** |

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Staffing shifted the most.** This tells us that in our model, staffing has the strongest connection to mortality. If you can only investigate one thing, start with staffing.

This is the power of running the model backwards -- it tells you *where to look first*.
:::


## The Updating Rule in Plain English

::: {.definition-box}
**Belief Updating (Bayes' Rule in Plain English)**

1. Start with your best guess about a cause (the prior)
2. Ask: "How likely is the evidence I just observed, under each possible state of the cause?"
3. The state that makes the evidence *more likely* gets a boost; the other state gets downgraded
4. Normalize so your beliefs still add up to 100%

That is it. That is all Bayes' rule does.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
You have already seen the formal math in Chapter 4. Here, we focus on the *logic*: evidence that is more likely under one explanation than another shifts your beliefs toward that explanation.
:::


# How Evidence Flows {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Revisiting the three triplets from Chapter 2</span>


## The Three Structures, Revisited

In Chapter 2, you learned three patterns that every causal diagram is built from. Now we ask a new question: **How does evidence travel through each one?**

. . .

| # | Name | Shape | Evidence Flow Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Chain** | A --> B --> C | Flows along the chain... unless B is known |
| 2 | **Fork** | A <-- B --> C | Flows through the common cause... unless B is known |
| 3 | **Collider** | A --> B <-- C | **BLOCKED** by default... unless B is known |

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
Chains and forks behave the same way: evidence flows freely, but conditioning on the middle node *blocks* it. Colliders are the rebel: evidence is blocked by default, but conditioning on the middle node *opens* it.
:::


## Chain: Evidence Flows Along the Path

<table style="width: 70%; margin: 0.5em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">Training</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">--> [+]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node">Competency</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">
<span class="dag-arrow negative">--> [-]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome">Mortality</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Competency is unknown:**

You learn that mortality is high. This is bad news about competency, which is bad news about training. Evidence flows the whole way along the chain.

"High mortality? Probably low competency. Probably inadequate training."
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Competency is known:**

You already know competency is low. Now learning that mortality is high tells you nothing *new* about training -- competency already explained everything.

The chain is **blocked**.
:::
:::
:::


## Fork: Evidence Flows Through the Common Cause

<table style="width: 75%; margin: 0.5em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome">PPH Detection</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive"><-- [+]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node confounder">Workforce Quality</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">--> [+]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome">Newborn Resuscitation</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Quality is unknown:**

A region is bad at PPH detection. This suggests low workforce quality, which suggests they are also bad at newborn resuscitation. Evidence flows through the common cause.

"Bad at PPH detection? Probably bad at resuscitation too."
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Quality is known:**

You already know workforce quality is good. Now learning about PPH detection tells you nothing new about resuscitation -- the common cause is accounted for.

The fork is **blocked**.
:::
:::
:::


## Collider: Evidence is BLOCKED by Default

<table style="width: 75%; margin: 0.5em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">Staffing</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">--> [+]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node" style="border-width: 3px;">Neonatal<br>Outcome</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive"><-- [+]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">Equipment</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Outcome is unknown:**

Staffing and equipment are independent decisions. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other. The collider **blocks** the flow.

"Staffing is low? That tells me nothing about equipment."
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Outcome is known:**

You learn the newborn survived. Now staffing and equipment are *connected* -- they compete to explain the good outcome. The collider is **opened**.

This is **explaining away**.
:::
:::
:::


## Summary: The Three Rules

::: {.key-takeaway}
**Burn these three rules into your memory:**

- **Chain (A --> B --> C):** Evidence flows... unless B is known. Then it stops.
- **Fork (A <-- B --> C):** Evidence flows... unless B is known. Then it stops.
- **Collider (A --> B <-- C):** Evidence is BLOCKED... unless B is known. Then it flows!

Chains and forks: conditioning blocks. Colliders: conditioning opens. The collider is the rebel.
:::


# Explaining Away -- The Crown Jewel {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">One cause explains away the other</span>


## The Setup

Here is a scenario that will stick with you.

. . .

::: {.example-block}
[A Newborn Survives Against the Odds]{.example-label}

A health facility in a remote Ethiopian region -- where outcomes are usually poor -- reports that a newborn with respiratory distress **survived**. This is great news, but surprising.

Two things could explain it:

- **Amazing staff** who performed skilled resuscitation
- **Great equipment** -- a functioning CPAP machine was available

Or maybe both.
:::

. . .

<table style="width: 70%; margin: 0.5em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">Staffing<br>Quality</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">--> [+]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node" style="border-width: 3px;">Newborn<br>Outcome</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive"><-- [+]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">Equipment<br>Quality</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>


## The Twist

You investigate further and learn that the CPAP machine was **broken** that day. The equipment was NOT available.

. . .

Now think about what happens to your belief about the staff.

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box}
**Before learning about equipment:**

"The baby survived. Could be good staff, could be good equipment, could be both."

P(Staff = Skilled) = moderately high
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**After learning equipment was broken:**

"The baby survived *without* equipment?! The staff must have been incredible."

P(Staff = Skilled) = **MUCH higher**
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**This is explaining away.** When you rule out one cause of a good outcome, you become *even more* convinced the other cause must be present. One explanation crowds out the other.
:::


## Why This Matters So Much

Explaining away is not just a curiosity. It changes how you diagnose problems.

. . .

::: {.example-block}
[The Reverse Direction]{.example-label}

A region has **high** neonatal mortality. You learn that staffing is actually **adequate**.

What happens to your belief about equipment?

**It gets worse.** If staffing is fine but outcomes are still bad, then equipment must be the problem. Good staffing "explains away" the possibility that staffing caused the bad outcome, leaving equipment as the prime suspect.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**The management insight:** Every time you confirm that one potential cause is in good shape, the spotlight shifts more intensely to the remaining causes. Explaining away focuses your attention.
:::


## Explaining Away: The Numbers

Let us make it concrete with a simplified model:

. . .

**Prior beliefs (before any evidence):**

- P(Staff = Skilled) = 40%
- P(Equipment = Available) = 35%

. . .

**Now we observe: the newborn survived.**

| Condition | P(Staff = Skilled) | P(Equipment = Available) |
|---|---|---|
| **Prior** (no evidence) | 40% | 35% |
| **Given survival** | 52% | 47% |
| **Given survival AND equipment broken** | **71%** | -- |
| **Given survival AND staff is unskilled** | -- | **68%** |

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Look at the jumps.** Knowing the baby survived raises both estimates modestly. But ruling out one cause makes the remaining cause shoot up dramatically. That is explaining away -- and it is the most powerful diagnostic tool in your toolkit.
:::


## Everyday Explaining Away

::: {.example-block}
[Examples You Already Know]{.example-label}

- **University admissions:** A student got into a top university. Was it grades or athletics? If you learn the student has average grades, you become *very* confident they are a star athlete.

- **A restaurant is packed.** Is the food amazing, or is it the only option nearby? If you learn there are ten other restaurants on the same block, you become *more* convinced the food must be exceptional.

- **Your internet is slow.** Is it your router or the provider? You restart the router and it is still slow. Now you are *much more sure* the problem is the provider.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
Explaining away happens every time two independent causes compete to explain the same result. It is everywhere once you start looking for it.
:::


# MNH Application: Diagnosing an Ethiopian Region {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Using the model to figure out what went wrong</span>


## Ethiopia: The Context

| Indicator | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) | ~28 per 1,000 live births | WHO |
| Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) | ~267 per 100,000 live births | WHO |
| Antenatal care coverage (1+ visit) | ~74% | DHS/WHO |
| Health Extension Workers | ~38,000+ across 8+ regions | Gov't of Ethiopia |
| Facility delivery rate | ~50% (wide regional variation) | DHS |
| Skilled birth attendance | ~28% (national, with huge regional gaps) | WHO |

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
Ethiopia has made remarkable progress through its Health Extension Worker (HEW) program, which deploys community health workers to rural areas. But regional variation is enormous -- some regions perform far better than others.
:::


## The Diagnostic Scenario

::: {.callout-box .red}
**Alert:** A region in rural Ethiopia reports NMR of 35 per 1,000 -- well above the national average. Despite receiving program resources, mortality has not improved. The program director asks: **"What is going wrong?"**
:::

. . .

**We will use our Bayesian network to diagnose the problem -- one piece of evidence at a time.**

. . .

**The model:**

<table style="width: 85%; margin: 0.3em auto; font-size: 0.45em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">HEW Staffing<br>(S)</div>
</td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">Equipment<br>(E)</div>
</td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">Referral<br>System (R)</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">|</span></td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">|</span></td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">|</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="5" style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;">
<div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em;">Quality of Care (Q)</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow negative">|</span></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome">Neonatal Mortality<br>Rate (NMR)</div>
</td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
</table>


## Step 1: Start with Priors

Before learning anything about this specific region, our best guesses come from national data:

. . .

| Variable | States | Prior |
|---|---|---|
| **HEW Staffing (S)** | Adequate / Low | 0.40 / 0.60 |
| **Equipment (E)** | Available / Unavailable | 0.35 / 0.65 |
| **Referral System (R)** | Functional / Weak | 0.30 / 0.70 |

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
These priors reflect typical conditions across Ethiopian regions -- roughly 40% of facilities have adequate HEW staffing, only 35% have functioning essential equipment, and about 30% have reliable referral pathways. These come from publicly available HMIS and survey data.
:::


## Step 2: First Evidence -- NMR is High

We observe: **NMR = High** (35/1,000).

. . .

Using the model, we update all three root causes:

| Variable | Prior | Posterior (NMR=High) | Shift |
|---|---|---|---|
| P(Staffing = Low) | 0.60 | **0.72** | +12 points |
| P(Equipment = Unavailable) | 0.65 | **0.74** | +9 points |
| P(Referral = Weak) | 0.70 | **0.78** | +8 points |

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**All three causes shifted toward their "bad" states.** This makes sense -- high mortality is more consistent with poor inputs than good inputs. But staffing shifted the most, suggesting it is the strongest suspect.
:::


## Step 3: Second Evidence -- Equipment is Adequate

A field visit reveals that equipment is actually in decent shape -- CPAP machines are available, essential drugs are stocked.

. . .

**Now we update again, adding this evidence:**

| Variable | After NMR=High only | After NMR=High AND Equip=Available | Shift |
|---|---|---|---|
| P(Staffing = Low) | 0.72 | **0.81** | +9 points |
| P(Referral = Weak) | 0.78 | **0.84** | +6 points |

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**Explaining away in action!** We ruled out equipment as the problem. But mortality is still high. So our belief that staffing and referrals are causing the problem *intensified*. Equipment being adequate makes the other causes *more* suspect, not less.
:::


## Step 4: Third Evidence -- Referral System is Functional

Deeper investigation shows the referral system actually works -- ambulances are available and the regional hospital accepts referrals promptly.

. . .

| Variable | After NMR=H + Equip OK | After NMR=H + Equip OK + Referral OK | Shift |
|---|---|---|---|
| P(Staffing = Low) | 0.81 | **0.91** | +10 points |

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**The diagnosis is clear.** We have ruled out equipment and referrals. The model now says there is a **91% probability** that staffing is the root cause. Each piece of evidence that ruled out an alternative cause made staffing *more* likely -- classic explaining away.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Recommendation:** Prioritize an HEW staffing review for this region. The model points to a workforce gap as the primary driver of high mortality, even though equipment and referrals appear adequate.
:::


## The Diagnosis Pathway -- Summary

<div class="step-flow">
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #005CB9;"><span class="step-number">1</span><br>Prior<br>P(Staff Low) = 60%</div>
<div class="step-arrow">--></div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #FA7650;"><span class="step-number orange">2</span><br>NMR is High<br>P(Staff Low) = 72%</div>
<div class="step-arrow">--></div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #F8A623;"><span class="step-number amber">3</span><br>Equip is OK<br>P(Staff Low) = 81%</div>
<div class="step-arrow">--></div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #E24A3F;"><span class="step-number red">4</span><br>Referral is OK<br>P(Staff Low) = 91%</div>
</div>

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**Notice the pattern:** Each time we *ruled out* a possible cause, the remaining causes became more suspect. This is explaining away applied sequentially -- a diagnostic workflow. The model did the hard reasoning for us.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**This is situational analysis.** You observe outcomes, gather evidence, and use the model to progressively narrow down the root cause. It is exactly what a good doctor does -- and now you can do it for an entire health system.
:::


# R Workshop {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Bayesian inference with bnlearn::cpquery()</span>


## R Block 1: Build the Ethiopian MNH Model

```{r}
#| label: bn-build
#| echo: true

# -------------------------------------------------------
# Chapter 5 R Workshop: Situational Analysis
# We build a Bayesian network for an Ethiopian region
# and use cpquery() to diagnose problems by running
# the model backwards.
# -------------------------------------------------------

library(bnlearn)

# Step 1: Define the DAG structure.
# [Staffing], [Equipment], [Referral] are root nodes (no parents).
# [Quality] depends on all three.
# [NMR] depends on Quality.
dag <- model2network(
  "[Staffing][Equipment][Referral][Quality|Staffing:Equipment:Referral][NMR|Quality]"
)

# Quick check: print the arcs to confirm the structure
arcs(dag)
# Should show 4 arcs:
#   Staffing  -> Quality
#   Equipment -> Quality
#   Referral  -> Quality
#   Quality   -> NMR
```


## R Block 2: Specify the CPTs

```{r}
#| label: bn-cpts
#| echo: true

# -------------------------------------------------------
# Root nodes: these are the prior probabilities.
# Based on publicly available Ethiopian health data.
# -------------------------------------------------------

# 40% of facilities have adequate HEW staffing
cpt_staffing <- array(c(0.40, 0.60), dim = 2,
  dimnames = list(Staffing = c("Adequate", "Low")))

# 35% have functioning essential equipment
cpt_equipment <- array(c(0.35, 0.65), dim = 2,
  dimnames = list(Equipment = c("Available", "Unavailable")))

# 30% have reliable referral pathways
cpt_referral <- array(c(0.30, 0.70), dim = 2,
  dimnames = list(Referral = c("Functional", "Weak")))

# -------------------------------------------------------
# Quality of Care depends on all three root nodes.
# 8 rows (2 x 2 x 2 parent combinations).
# Each row: P(Good), P(Poor). Rows must sum to 1.
# -------------------------------------------------------

cpt_quality <- array(
  c(
    # Staffing=Adequate, Equipment=Available, Referral=Functional
    0.92, 0.08,
    # Staffing=Low, Equipment=Available, Referral=Functional
    0.55, 0.45,
    # Staffing=Adequate, Equipment=Unavailable, Referral=Functional
    0.65, 0.35,
    # Staffing=Low, Equipment=Unavailable, Referral=Functional
    0.25, 0.75,
    # Staffing=Adequate, Equipment=Available, Referral=Weak
    0.78, 0.22,
    # Staffing=Low, Equipment=Available, Referral=Weak
    0.40, 0.60,
    # Staffing=Adequate, Equipment=Unavailable, Referral=Weak
    0.50, 0.50,
    # Staffing=Low, Equipment=Unavailable, Referral=Weak
    0.12, 0.88
  ),
  dim = c(2, 2, 2, 2),
  dimnames = list(
    Quality   = c("Good", "Poor"),
    Staffing  = c("Adequate", "Low"),
    Equipment = c("Available", "Unavailable"),
    Referral  = c("Functional", "Weak")
  )
)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# NMR depends on Quality only.
# Good quality -> mostly low mortality.
# Poor quality -> mostly high mortality.
# -------------------------------------------------------

cpt_nmr <- array(
  c(0.85, 0.15,   # Quality = Good
    0.30, 0.70),  # Quality = Poor
  dim = c(2, 2),
  dimnames = list(
    NMR     = c("Low", "High"),
    Quality = c("Good", "Poor")
  )
)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# Combine everything into a fitted Bayesian network
# -------------------------------------------------------

bn_ethiopia <- custom.fit(dag, list(
  Staffing  = cpt_staffing,
  Equipment = cpt_equipment,
  Referral  = cpt_referral,
  Quality   = cpt_quality,
  NMR       = cpt_nmr
))
```


## R Block 3: Baseline Query -- What Do We Expect?

```{r}
#| label: bn-baseline
#| echo: true

# -------------------------------------------------------
# QUERY 1: What is the overall P(NMR = High)?
# This is the marginal -- averaging across all
# possible staffing, equipment, and referral states.
# "Before we learn anything, what is our best guess?"
# -------------------------------------------------------

cpquery(bn_ethiopia,
  event    = (NMR == "High"),
  evidence = TRUE,            # No evidence -- marginal query
  n = 1e6                     # Use 1 million samples for accuracy
)
# Expected: approximately 0.42
# "About a 42% chance of high NMR in a random region."
```

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**What cpquery() does:** It simulates a million hypothetical regions from the model, then counts how many have NMR = High. The fraction is the marginal probability. The `evidence = TRUE` means "no conditions -- just give me the overall average."
:::


## R Block 4: Running the Model Backwards

```{r}
#| label: bn-backwards
#| echo: true

# -------------------------------------------------------
# QUERY 2: We observe NMR = High.
# "What does this tell us about staffing?"
# This is the detective question -- reasoning backwards.
# -------------------------------------------------------

cpquery(bn_ethiopia,
  event    = (Staffing == "Low"),
  evidence = (NMR == "High"),
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: approximately 0.72
# Prior was 0.60; posterior is ~0.72.
# "High mortality makes low staffing more likely."

# -------------------------------------------------------
# QUERY 3: Same question for equipment.
# -------------------------------------------------------

cpquery(bn_ethiopia,
  event    = (Equipment == "Unavailable"),
  evidence = (NMR == "High"),
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: approximately 0.74
# Prior was 0.65; posterior is ~0.74.

# -------------------------------------------------------
# QUERY 4: And for the referral system.
# -------------------------------------------------------

cpquery(bn_ethiopia,
  event    = (Referral == "Weak"),
  evidence = (NMR == "High"),
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: approximately 0.78
# Prior was 0.70; posterior is ~0.78.
```


## R Block 5: Explaining Away in Action

```{r}
#| label: bn-explaining-away
#| echo: true

# -------------------------------------------------------
# QUERY 5: Explaining away!
# NMR is high AND equipment is OK.
# "What happens to our belief about staffing?"
# -------------------------------------------------------

cpquery(bn_ethiopia,
  event    = (Staffing == "Low"),
  evidence = (NMR == "High" & Equipment == "Available"),
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: approximately 0.81
# Was 0.72 with just NMR=High.
# Ruling out equipment made staffing MORE suspect!

# -------------------------------------------------------
# QUERY 6: Full explaining away.
# NMR is high, equipment is OK, AND referral is OK.
# Now staffing is the only suspect left.
# -------------------------------------------------------

cpquery(bn_ethiopia,
  event    = (Staffing == "Low"),
  evidence = (NMR == "High" &
              Equipment == "Available" &
              Referral == "Functional"),
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: approximately 0.91
# The more causes we rule out, the more certain
# we become about the remaining cause.
# This is explaining away -- the crown jewel.
```


## R Block 6: Comparing Two Regions

```{r}
#| label: bn-compare
#| echo: true

# -------------------------------------------------------
# Compare a struggling region (NMR=High) with a
# well-performing one (NMR=Low).
# "What does the model infer about each?"
# -------------------------------------------------------

compare_regions <- function(bn, nmr_state) {
  data.frame(
    Variable = c("P(Staffing=Low)",
                 "P(Equipment=Unavail)",
                 "P(Referral=Weak)"),
    Prior = c(0.60, 0.65, 0.70),
    Posterior = c(
      cpquery(bn, (Staffing == "Low"),
              (NMR == nmr_state), n = 1e6),
      cpquery(bn, (Equipment == "Unavailable"),
              (NMR == nmr_state), n = 1e6),
      cpquery(bn, (Referral == "Weak"),
              (NMR == nmr_state), n = 1e6)
    )
  )
}

# Struggling region
cat("=== Region with High NMR ===\n")
high_region <- compare_regions(bn_ethiopia, "High")
high_region$Shift <- high_region$Posterior - high_region$Prior
print(high_region)

# Well-performing region
cat("\n=== Region with Low NMR ===\n")
low_region <- compare_regions(bn_ethiopia, "Low")
low_region$Shift <- low_region$Posterior - low_region$Prior
print(low_region)

# The shifts should go in opposite directions:
# High NMR -> causes shift toward "bad" states
# Low NMR  -> causes shift toward "good" states
```


## R Block 7: Visualize the Belief Updating

```{r}
#| label: bn-viz
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

library(ggplot2)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# Visualize how beliefs shift as evidence accumulates.
# This shows the "explaining away" diagnostic pathway.
# -------------------------------------------------------

pathway <- data.frame(
  Step = factor(
    c("1. Prior", "2. NMR=High", "3. + Equip OK", "4. + Referral OK"),
    levels = c("1. Prior", "2. NMR=High", "3. + Equip OK", "4. + Referral OK")
  ),
  P_Staffing_Low = c(0.60, 0.72, 0.81, 0.91)
)

ggplot(pathway, aes(x = Step, y = P_Staffing_Low)) +
  geom_col(fill = c("#005CB9", "#FA7650", "#F8A623", "#E24A3F"),
           width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(P_Staffing_Low * 100, "%")),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent,
                     limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Explaining Away: P(Staffing = Low) as Evidence Accumulates",
    subtitle = "Each ruled-out cause makes staffing MORE suspect",
    x = NULL,
    y = "P(Staffing = Low)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#005CB9", face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#666")
  )
```


## Key Takeaways

::: {.key-takeaway}
**Situational analysis means running the model backwards -- from outcomes to causes.**

Three skills make it work:

1. **Average across possibilities** when you do not know a variable (marginal probability)
2. **Update your best guess** when new evidence arrives (belief updating)
3. **Understand how evidence flows** through chains, forks, and colliders -- especially explaining away
:::

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- **Marginal probability** = "What is my best guess before I learn anything?" (a weighted average)
- **Belief updating** = "How does my best guess change when I learn something new?"
- **Chains and forks** let evidence flow, but conditioning on the middle node blocks it
- **Colliders** block evidence by default, but conditioning on the collision point opens the flow
- **Explaining away** is the most powerful diagnostic tool: ruling out one cause makes the remaining causes *more* likely
- **In R**, `cpquery()` lets you ask any backward question with a single line of code
:::


## Looking Ahead

::: {.callout-box}
**Next: Chapter 6 -- Simpson's Paradox and Cost-Effectiveness**

Now that you can run the model backwards, we tackle a famous trap:

- **Simpson's Paradox** -- when aggregated data reverses the true causal effect
- Why an intervention can look *harmful* overall but be *beneficial* in every subgroup
- How conditioning on the wrong variable produces disastrously wrong conclusions
- Practical implications for how large MNH programs evaluate their country portfolios
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**The connection:** Chapter 5 taught you to diagnose *what went wrong* in a single region. Chapter 6 teaches you to avoid a deadly statistical illusion when comparing *across* regions -- an illusion that has led to real-world policy failures in global health.
:::
